title: Given a `List<Employee>`, collect the results of a stream into a list that cannot be modified afterwards, using either `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()` or `Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)`.
shortTitle: Collect employees into an unmodifiable list using toUnmodifiableList or collectingAndThen with Collections.unmodifiableList
keyPoints: Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() (Java 10+) returns a truly immutable list with no backing reference leaked
collectingAndThen(toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList) is the Java 8 portable alternative
Both throw UnsupportedOperationException on add, remove, set, and clear
toUnmodifiableList() rejects null elements and throws NullPointerException if any are present
Stream.toList() (Java 16+) also returns an unmodifiable list and is the most concise option
Returning unmodifiable collections from service methods prevents callers from mutating shared state

s1_definition.oneliner: Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() collects stream results into an immutable list that throws UnsupportedOperationException on any modification attempt.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **toUnmodifiableList()** – (Java 10+) collects into a genuinely immutable list with no backing mutable reference.
- **collectingAndThen(toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)** – the Java 8 form that collects into a mutable ArrayList, then wraps it in an unmodifiable view.
- **Stream.toList()** – (Java 16+) the shortest form: `stream.toList()` returns an unmodifiable list.
- **Null rejection** – `toUnmodifiableList()` throws `NullPointerException` if any element is null, consistent with `List.of()`.
- **Defensive design** – returning unmodifiable lists from service methods prevents callers from mutating shared internal state.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India produces a finalized list of approved high-value account holders. She laminates the printout before distributing it. The laminated list is the unmodifiable collection: everyone can read it, but no one can add or remove a name. The `toUnmodifiableList()` method is the lamination step.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Stream<Employee>
       │
       │  .map(Employee::getName)
       ▼
  Stream<String>
       │
       │  .collect(toUnmodifiableList())
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Unmodifiable List<String>              │
  │  [Rajesh, Priya, Amit, Kavita, ...]     │
  │                                         │
  │  .add(x)    → UnsupportedOperationEx    │
  │  .remove(x) → UnsupportedOperationEx    │
  │  .set(i, x) → UnsupportedOperationEx    │
  │  .clear()   → UnsupportedOperationEx    │
  │  .get(i)    → OK (read allowed)         │
  │  .size()    → OK (read allowed)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Collecting a stream into an unmodifiable list prevents callers from adding, removing, or replacing elements after collection. On Java 10+, `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()` produces a truly immutable list with no backing reference. On Java 8, `collectingAndThen(toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)` wraps a mutable ArrayList in a read-only view. On Java 16+, `Stream.toList()` is the most concise option.

The key distinction is that `toUnmodifiableList()` rejects null elements (throws NullPointerException), while `Stream.toList()` and the `collectingAndThen` form allow nulls. The common mistake is assuming `Collectors.toList()` returns an unmodifiable list. It returns a mutable ArrayList.

In banking systems, returning unmodifiable lists from service methods is a defensive design practice. The compliance list of high-value account holders flows through audit, notification, and reporting components. Making it unmodifiable prevents any downstream component from accidentally adding or removing entries.

Remember one sentence: toUnmodifiableList makes the collected result read-only and null-free, while Stream.toList (Java 16+) is shorter but allows nulls.
